source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Which search method wins depends on question difficulty. On easy questions parallel best-of-N beats beam search at large budgets. On hard questions beam search against a process reward model beats best-of-N. Gap 1 and 3: there is no single best search; the operator must be chosen per item.
numbers: PaLM 2-S*, MATH. Compute-optimal choice by difficulty bin matched best-of-N with about 4x less test-time compute (revisions and PRM search). Against a FLOPs-matched 14x larger model: test-time compute wins on easy and medium questions; pretraining wins on the hardest questions when inference load is high.
quote: beam search is more effective on harder questions
limits: Needs a trained PRM and a difficulty estimate; one model family from 2024; maths only (checkable answer). Not an equal-token test against a modern reasoning model.
agent_relevance: S6 should not be always-on. Estimate difficulty first, spend branching only when the item is hard, otherwise sample or revise sequentially.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Deeper search over a learned verifier is exploited by the generator. Lookahead search (closest to MCTS) generally underperforms plain beam search and best-of-N at the same generation budget. Beam search degrades on easy questions as budget grows (verifier over-optimisation). Gap 4.
numbers: Beam search is best at small budgets, then gains shrink and it falls below best-of-N as budget grows. Lookahead underperforms at equal generation budget. Easy levels 1-2: beam search degrades relative to best-of-N; levels 3-4: beam consistently beats best-of-N.
quote: lookahead-search generally underperforms other methods at the same generation budget
limits: Verifier is a trained PRM, not a code check; maths only.
agent_relevance: The weak scorer is the limit, not search depth. Prefer code or held-out checks in the loop; cap search depth when the scorer is a model (G7).

source: Wu et al. (2025) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for LLM Problem-Solving
finding: Compared greedy, majority vote, best-of-n, weighted vote, MCTS and a cheaper tree search (REBASE) at equal compute. MCTS costs far more tokens per final answer because most tree paths are spent on node estimation. Gap 1 (token-matched comparison).
numbers: MATH500 and GSM8K. Llemma-7B with REBASE beat Llemma-34B across all tested strategies; the 7B model outperformed 34B until 128 7B solutions were sampled. Paper says MCTS needs dozens of times more generated tokens than simpler methods and did not do well with weighted voting.
quote: MCTS consumes substantially more resources, often requiring dozens of times more generated tokens than simpler methods
limits: Pythia, Llemma and Mistral-class models, 2024; reward-model scored; maths with known answers.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens, expensive tree search can lose to cheap sampling plus voting. Keep S6 budgeted and always compare with best-of-N at equal tokens (G7).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Repeated sampling raises coverage log-linearly over four orders of magnitude, but it turns into accuracy only where an automatic verifier exists. Without one, majority vote and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples. Gap 2.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples), above the 43% single-sample state of the art at the time. GSM8K and MATH coverage is reported with an oracle verifier; no-verifier selection plateaus.
quote: In domains without automatic verifiers, we find that common methods for picking from a sample collection plateau beyond several hundred samples
limits: Coverage is pass@k with a perfect checker on code and proofs; says nothing about taste-judged tasks.
agent_relevance: Gains come from the check, not from search itself. Where no check exists, give the sub-step one (tests, simulator, constraint ledger) before spending samples.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
finding: Controlled puzzles at matched inference compute show three regimes. Low complexity: the non-thinking model equals or beats the thinking model with fewer tokens. Medium: the thinking model wins. High: both collapse to zero. Gap 1 on 2025 models.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking vs non-thinking and DeepSeek-R1 vs V3, up to 64k tokens, 25 samples per model, puzzle and complexity level. On MATH500 pass@k of thinking and non-thinking is comparable at the same token budget; the gap widens on AIME24 and more on AIME25.
quote: non-thinking models are capable of obtaining performance comparable to, or even better than thinking models with more token-efficient inference
limits: Puzzle environments; 25 samples per cell; others have criticised token-limit and solvability confounds (not opened here).
agent_relevance: A strong reasoning model's own chain of thought is not beaten by outside search at medium complexity, and nothing beats the collapse at high complexity. Route by complexity; do not add search to easy items.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking (failure analysis)
finding: Reasoning-model failure is partly fixation on an early wrong answer and partly poor step execution. In failed cases the model often fixates on an early wrong answer and wastes the rest of its budget. Giving the exact algorithm in the prompt did not move the collapse point. Gap 3.
numbers: Near the collapse point thinking tokens fall as complexity rises despite spare budget. Providing the algorithm for Tower of Hanoi and Checker Jumping: accuracy did not improve; collapse at about the same size.
quote: In failed cases, it often fixates on an early wrong answers, wasting the remaining token budget
limits: Descriptive; no operator ablation at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Supports an outside controller that forces an alternative branch after an early commitment, and a code executor for exact steps.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI's o1 on PlanBench
finding: o1-preview nearly solves plain Blocksworld but much less of the obfuscated version, and falls apart on long plans. So part of earlier gains was surface-form recall. Gap 10.
numbers: 600 instances. Blocksworld 97.8% (o1-preview), 56.6% (o1-mini). Mystery Blocksworld 52.8% and 19.1%. Randomized Mystery 37.3% (o1-preview). 110 larger problems (20-40 step plans): 23.63%. Fast Downward 100% on all, in 0.265 s versus 40 to 111 s for o1-preview. Unsolvable instances: only 27% correctly flagged as unsolvable (16% on randomized mystery).
quote: Far surpassing any LLM, o1 correctly answers 97.8% of these instances
limits: One model family, early preview, a week after release.
agent_relevance: Run obfuscated copies of every test item and report the drop. The plain versus obfuscated gap estimates the recall share.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) PlanBench Table 1 (pre-reasoning LLMs)
finding: Pre-reasoning LLMs score 8 to 63% on Blocksworld but 0 to 4.3% on Mystery Blocksworld, the same problems with names obfuscated. Gap 10; confirms K09.
numbers: One-shot Blocksworld: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 57.6%, GPT-4 34.3%, LLaMA 3.1 405B 47.3%. One-shot Mystery: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 3.1%, GPT-4 4.3%, LLaMA 3.1 405B 3.5%. Zero-shot Blocksworld best is LLaMA 3.1 405B at 62.6%; zero-shot Mystery is 0 to 0.8% for most models. GPT-4 zero-shot Blocksworld is 34.6% in this table.
limits: 600 instances per cell; 2024 models. The earlier ~12% GPT-4 figure (b21) is not in this table, so the two numbers still differ by source.
agent_relevance: Any claim that search or a scaffold helps must be re-measured on a relabelled version of the same item.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: Self-critique loses accuracy; sound external verification gains it; and most of the gain survives with no critique content at all, just re-prompting. Gap 1, 3, 4.
numbers: GPT-4, 100 instances per domain. Standard prompting / LLM+LLM critique / LLM+sound verifier: Game of 24 5% / 3% / 36-38%; Graph Coloring 16% / 2% / 34-38%; Blocksworld 40% / 55% / 83-87%; Mystery Blocksworld 4% / 0% / 6-10%. Sampling with a sound verifier and no critique: Game of 24 28% (k=15) and 42% (k=25); self-consistency 6%.
quote: significant performance collapse with self-critique and significant performance gains with sound external verification
limits: GPT-4 from 2023; formal tasks with sound verifiers. Self-critique on Blocksworld went up (40 to 55%), so the result is not uniform.
agent_relevance: The verifier matters more than the critic text. Wire code checks into every loop and drop critique prose that does not change outcomes.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: Cost-matched check of ToT: with a sound verifier and 150 plain queries (cost equal to ToT) GPT-4 reaches 70% on Game of 24, close to ToT's 74%. So ToT's edge over sampling shrinks to 4 points once sampling is paired with a sound check. Gap 1; refines K04.
numbers: ToT cost $0.74 per problem, equal to about 150 CoT prompts at $0.47 per 100. 150 direct queries plus sound verifier: 70% vs ToT 74% as reported by Yao et al.
quote: ToT implements a classical breadth-first search algorithm, only prompting the LLM to generate (much easier) intermediate steps
limits: The comparison gives sampling a verifier that ToT does not use. Single domain; 100 instances.
agent_relevance: S6 beats unverified sampling but only slightly beats verified sampling at equal cost on a crisp task. Put the code check first, search second.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: A model verifier loses correct answers. On Game of 24 without chain of thought it rejected about one in five of the true-correct answers. Gap 4.
numbers: Game of 24 verifier: overall accuracy 87.0% (3567 of 4100); 10.4% (320 of 3071) of wrong answers accepted; 20.7% (213 of 1029) of correct answers rejected (column mapping inferred from the table text). Giving the verifier chain of thought raised Game of 24 accuracy to 98.8%.
quote: verifier LLM's false negative rate is significant across our domains
limits: PDF table layouts for the other domains were garbled; only the Game of 24 row is quoted. The column mapping is my reading.
agent_relevance: Never let a model alone prune a branch it scored low. Require a code or held-out check before discarding, or keep rejected branches in a reserve.

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Best-first tree search in a real web environment lifts a GPT-4o agent, and the gain grows with search budget. This is the closest opened test on an open-ended task with an outside outcome check, though the search itself uses a model value function. Gap 2.
numbers: VisualWebArena: GPT-4o + SoM 18.9% to 26.4% (+39.7% relative). WebArena: 15.0% to 19.2% (+28.0%). Llama-3-70B on VWA: 7.6% to 16.7% (+119.7%); on WebArena 7.6% to 10.1%. Depth and breadth ablation on 200 VWA tasks: d=1,b=1 24.5%, rising to 37.0% (+51%) at the largest tree tested.
quote: best-first tree search that operates within the actual environment space
limits: Tasks have a programmatic success check at the end, so they are not taste-judged. Search costs several times more model calls than the baseline.
agent_relevance: Evidence that S6 can pay off in open, long-horizon work when the final verdict is exact, and that budget should grow in both depth and breadth together.

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: The value function is the bottleneck. A better scorer gives most of the gain, a perfect one gives the most. Gap 4.
numbers: Success rate on 200 VWA tasks by value function: none 24.5%; LLaVA-v1.6-34B with self-consistency n=20 30.0%; GPT-4o without self-consistency 28.5%; GPT-4o with SC n=5 32.5%; GPT-4o with SC n=20 37.0%; ground-truth reward 43.5%.
quote: self-consistency is essential for good performance
limits: Subset of 200 tasks, single run per cell; no confidence intervals in the text read.
agent_relevance: Self-consistency on the scorer (n=20) is worth +8.5 points here. A held-out code check is the upper bound and should replace the model score wherever possible.

source: Xie et al. (2024) TravelPlanner: A Benchmark for Real-World Planning with Language Agents
finding: Multi-constraint planning with 1,225 intents (180 validation, 1,000 test) exposes forgotten constraints. GPT-4-Turbo with ReAct passes 0.6% of tasks; all other LLMs 0%. Models pass individual constraints but rarely all of them. Gap 5 (no ledger test, but this measures the failure a ledger is meant to cure).
numbers: Test set, two-stage mode, GPT-4-Turbo: delivery 93.1%, commonsense pass micro 63.3% / macro 2.0%, hard-constraint pass micro 10.5% / macro 5.5%, final pass 0.6%. Greedy search baseline: delivery 100%, final pass 0%. Two-stage scores fall below sole-planning scores by up to over 30 points.
quote: GPT-4 successfully produces a plan that meets all the constraints for a few tasks (0.6%)
limits: 2024 models; the paper does not test an outside constraint tracker. Later symbolic-checker systems on this benchmark were not opened.
agent_relevance: The micro versus macro gap is the argument for a code-held constraint ledger: each constraint is usually satisfiable alone, joint satisfaction fails. Test ledger vs no ledger on a TravelPlanner subset.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)
finding: Within one model, open-ended answers repeat even at high temperature and with min-p decoding, so sampling knobs do not buy diversity. Gap 6 (K15 confirmed).
numbers: 25 models x 100 open-ended queries x 50 responses at top-p 0.9, T=1.0: in 79% of cases average pairwise similarity exceeds 0.8. Min-p (min-p 0.1, T=2.0, top-p 1.0): similarity among responses to the same prompt typically still exceeds 0.8; 81% of pairs exceed 0.7 and 61.2% exceed 0.8 in the min-p run. Dataset: 26K queries, 31,250 human annotations, 25 raters per item.
quote: even under maximally aggressive sampling, LMs still fail to generate diverse responses to open-ended queries
limits: Similarity is measured with text-embedding-3-small; similarity is not novelty or quality. Models are 2024 to early 2025 vintage.
agent_relevance: A forced-diversity step must act at the prompt or structure level (name different families first), not through temperature. Measure embedding similarity and quality together.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)
finding: Different models give similar answers, so an ensemble of sibling models gives less diversity than expected. Gap 6.
numbers: Average pairwise similarity between responses from different models ranges from 71% to 82%. DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81. Reward models and LM judges are less well calibrated to human ratings on items where annotators disagree.
quote: model ensembles may not yield true diversity when their constituents share overlapping alignment and training priors
limits: Does not test whether a diversity operator raises group diversity or solution quality; no verified task.
agent_relevance: Do not count samples from sibling models as independent branches in S6. Branch by structure (different solution families) and check embedding distance across branches.

source: Oswald et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Planning Domain Generators
finding: LLMs can write a planning domain (predicates, actions, preconditions) from text with some success, but only a quarter reach functional equivalence. Gap 9: formulation is a real failure source, though measured only on small classic domains.
numbers: 7 LLMs, 9 planning domains, 3 description classes. Best model LLaMA-2-70b produced valid PDDL in 94% of domains and reconstructed 25% of domains as heuristically equivalent (top-100 plans from the K planner, 2 problems per domain). Equivalence depended largely on model size.
quote: exhibit a moderate level of proficiency in generating correct planning domains from natural language descriptions
limits: Old models, toy domains, equivalence judged by plan overlap, not design-sized problems. Not a design brief.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a one-shot formulation step. Check that the stated goal test and operators reproduce a known plan, and keep the original text for re-check.
